body:
## Everyone quotes the multiple. Nobody does the division.

Ask most people why their office has fixed height desks and you'll get some version of the same answer: the sit-stand ones cost twice as much.

That's true. It's also the least useful way to look at it.

Twice as much sounds like a decision that needs a board paper. Then you find out the actual difference is a few hundred dollars per person, spread across a five-year lease, and you realise you've been having the wrong conversation for years.

If you're specifying [office furniture in Newcastle](/blog/office-furniture-newcastle) this year, here are the real numbers.

## What desks actually cost

Supply pricing per workstation, excluding GST:

| Specification | Fixed height | Electric height adjustable |
|---|---|---|
| Entry level | $200 | $300 |
| What we normally specify | $300 | $600–$800 |
| Back to back cluster (2 person pod) | $600–$800 | $1,400–$1,600 |

Two things jump out of that table.

One: an entry-level electric height adjustable desk costs less than a mid-spec fixed desk. Three hundred dollars against three hundred dollars. If entry-level is where your budget sits, the height adjustable version is not a stretch — it's the same money.

Two: at the specification most offices actually land on, the difference is $300 to $500 a person.

Spread that across a five-year lease and it's $60 to $100 a year. Somewhere between one and two dollars a week, per employee. About one flat white a month.

That's the number. Not "twice the price."

## Why the price came down

The electric actuators inside the frame used to be a specialist component. They're now made at enormous volume for a global market, and dual-motor frames that were premium items a decade ago are ordinary commercial stock today.

The multiple hasn't collapsed. A height adjustable desk is still roughly double a fixed one at most specifications. What changed is the base — when the fixed desk is $300 instead of $900, doubling it stops being a budget problem.

Commercial ranges we specify regularly, including Desky, which our supply partner EOF Group stocks in Lambton, sit right in that band with proper commercial warranties behind them.

*(Pricing is supply only, excluding GST, and depends on tops, finishes, volume and lead time. Delivery and installation are quoted separately. Get a scoped quote before you set a budget.)*

## Back to back clusters — where most Newcastle offices land

Most professional services floors here run back-to-back pods rather than single desks. Better use of a floor plate, shared cable management, and screens between positions.

At $600 to $800 for a fixed two-person pod against $1,400 to $1,600 electric, you're looking at roughly $400 per person more.

Over a five-year lease, that's about $1.50 a week per employee. Worth saying plainly: run that against your rent. If you're paying Newcastle CBD rates across a floor, the entire furniture upgrade for the whole office is a rounding error next to one month's rent. It's the cheapest line item in your fit out with the most daily contact.

## The WHS argument is now the strongest one

This isn't a wellness perk. It's a hazard the national regulator has named.

Safe Work Australia treats prolonged sitting as a work health and safety risk in its own right. Their guidance is that more than about seven hours a day of sedentary time is too much, that the health effects don't disappear just because someone goes to the gym after work, and that workstations should be designed so people can change posture through the day. They're explicit that this belongs in the early planning stages of good work design.

Read that with your fit out program in mind. Early planning stages. That's now.

Specifying height adjustable at fit out costs you three to five hundred dollars a person. Retrofitting one desk at a time in year three — after a medical certificate or a claim — costs you the full desk, disposal of the old one, a separate install visit, and a floor that no longer matches.

You have a duty under the *Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (NSW)* to provide a safe working environment. Height adjustable desks aren't legally mandated. But when the regulator has published guidance saying design workstations so posture can vary, the cheapest possible time to act on it is before the order goes in.

## The staff argument nobody puts in the budget

Here's the part that doesn't appear on a spreadsheet.

Everyone in your office had a home setup for a couple of years. A lot of them bought their own sit-stand desk with their own money. They know what it feels like to stand up for the afternoon block when their back has had enough.

Asking those people to come in and sit at a fixed slab for eight hours is a small daily reminder that the office is worse than home. You won't hear about it in an exit interview. You'll feel it in how many days a week people choose to come in.

And when you're hiring, the office tour is part of the pitch. A floor of height adjustable desks reads as a business that spent money on its people. A floor of fixed desks reads as a business that spent money on reception. Candidates notice. In a Newcastle professional services market where the same fifteen firms compete for the same accountants, planners and engineers, that's not nothing.

That's an opinion, not a statistic. But it's an opinion formed from walking through a lot of offices.

## The honest counter-argument

A height adjustable desk that never gets raised is just a desk that cost you an extra three hundred dollars.

The research on this is fairly clear and fairly boring: the benefit comes from breaking up sitting time, not from owning the furniture. Buy fifty of them, say nothing on day one, and in six months a good portion of your floor will have used the up button twice.

So if you're spending the money, spend twenty minutes with it too:

- Set each desk on day one. Don't leave people to guess. Elbows at roughly ninety degrees, monitor top at eye level, feet flat.
- Give people a rhythm. Alternating every 45 to 60 minutes works better than "use it whenever."
- Have the leadership team stand. Nobody wants to be the only person standing in an open plan office. If the partners never raise theirs, nobody raises theirs.
- Anti-fatigue mats for anyone standing regularly on hard floors — common in Newcastle's refurbished CBD stock.

That's the difference between a spend and an outcome.

## When fixed height still makes sense

Not every position needs one. Fixed height is still right for:

- Hot desks and touchdown points used for under an hour at a time
- Reception and front-of-house joinery, usually custom built anyway
- Meeting and collaboration tables
- A genuinely tight budget where the money is better in the chairs. If you can only fund one, fund the task chairs. A bad chair does more damage than a fixed desk. Though at $300 for an entry-level electric, that trade-off comes up less often than it used to.

A sensible middle path: height adjustable across permanent desk positions, fixed height for the flexible ones. Most Newcastle offices we look at land around 70/30.

## What to check before you order

- Frame type. Dual motor, not single. Single motor frames are slower, less stable at height and wobble with two monitors on them.
- Weight capacity and stability at full extension. Ask for the tested rating, not the marketing number.
- Cable management. A desk that moves needs a cable basket and enough slack, or the first raise drags a monitor off the back edge. This gets missed constantly, especially on back-to-back pods where cabling is shared.
- Anti-collision. Worth having on a floor with pedestals and bins under desks.
- Warranty terms. Commercial warranty, not household. Check what specifically covers the motor.
- Lead time. Allow 4–8 weeks for stocked commercial ranges. Order once the floor plan is settled, not once the builder finishes.

## Frequently asked questions

**How much more do height adjustable desks cost than fixed height?**

At entry level, about $100 more per desk — roughly $200 fixed against $300 electric. At the specification most offices choose, around $300 to $500 more per person. For back-to-back two-person pods, expect $600–$800 fixed against $1,400–$1,600 electric. All supply only, excluding GST.

**Is a height adjustable desk worth it for a small office?**

The absolute cost is what matters, not the multiple. On a ten-person floor the upgrade is a few thousand dollars once, spread over a lease term of five years or more. It's usually the smallest line item in a fit out.

**Are height adjustable desks required under Australian WHS law?**

No. There's no legal requirement to provide them. But Safe Work Australia identifies prolonged sitting as a work health and safety risk and advises designing workstations so workers can vary posture, and employers have a general duty to provide a safe working environment under the *Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (NSW)*.

**Should every desk in the office be height adjustable?**

Not necessarily. It makes most sense for permanent positions where people sit for hours. Hot desks, touchdown points and meeting tables are usually fine at fixed height.

**Do people actually use standing desks?**

Only if you set them up and give them a rhythm. Usage drops sharply where desks are installed with no induction. Twenty minutes of setup on day one is what separates a useful desk from an expensive one.

**How long do height adjustable desks take to arrive in Newcastle?**

Allow 4–8 weeks from order to installation for stocked commercial ranges. Custom tops and made-to-order finishes take longer.

## The short version

The reason fixed height became the default is gone. At entry level the height adjustable version now costs the same as a mid-spec fixed desk. At the specification most offices choose, the difference is a dollar or two a week per person across a lease term. The regulator has named sitting as a risk you're meant to design around at the planning stage. And your staff already know what the alternative feels like, because they had one at home.
